paras: The lynching of an unidentified man near Woodville, Mississippi, took place in late May 1903, when, according to a wire report, citizens of Wilkinson County lynched a Black man described as a burglar who had confessed to setting fire to a store in Woodville. The victim's name was never given in the coverage found, and the case survives mainly as a one-line news item and as an entry in white and Black lynching tallies for 1903.

On a Friday morning early in May, a fire destroyed the brick dry goods store of C. Schaefer and the hardware store of G. A. Wettlin in Woodville, and goods were removed from the grocery of M. W. Brown, whom the Woodville Republican called "a respected colored merchant." The paper put the losses at $32,000, $10,000 and $300, noted that both main stores had burned before, and blamed "the dirty, villainous work of the fire bug." Residents subscribed a reward "for the arrest and conviction of the perpetrator," and the editor wrote that the account "makes the blood boil." No report found connects the lynched man to this particular fire by name or date.

A national news digest that ran on May 30 stated that "Citizens of Wilkinson county, Mississippi, lynched a negro burglar who confessed to setting fire to a store in Woodville." The item gave no name, no date, no number of participants and no method of killing. Lynching lists published that summer placed the killing "near Woodville" and dated it May 28, with the Wichita Searchlight recording the charge as arson.
No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage found, and the Woodville Republican's indexed pages for late May and early June carry no account of the lynching.

White coverage consisted of the single digest line, reprinted in the Willmar Tribune on May 30, The Tomahawk on June 4 and Fair Play of Ste. Genevieve, Missouri, on June 6, set among strikes, storms and other national news. In July a half-year tally credited to the Providence Journal, reprinted in the Indianapolis Journal and the Waterbury Evening Democrat, listed the victim only as "Unknown, colored, near Woodville, Miss." among forty-five lynchings.

Black papers likewise knew the case only as a line in a list. The Wichita Searchlight printed it on July 25 as "Unknown Negre, arson, near Woodville, Miss.," while the Seattle Republican, on August 7, included it under the heading "Mobocracy's Bloody Reign," introducing the list as a record that "Russia and Turkey might do well to emulate." Neither press published a narrative of the killing, and the man's name did not appear in either.

reader.title: Lynching of an unidentified man near Woodville, Mississippi (1903)
bases: The wire digest says citizens of Wilkinson county 'lynched' a Black man accused of arson and burglary, and white and Black lynching tallies count him (A3, A7, A9, A10).

The papers report that 'citizens' lynched a man accused of setting fire to a store and that lynching tallies counted his death (A3, A7, A9), which supports an illegal killing under a crime pretext; no report gives the size of the group or how he was killed.

The only narrative is one wire digest line reprinted in three papers (A3, A4, A5); the white and Black lynching lists (A7, A9, A10) add the month, the day 28 and 'arson' but may draw on the same report, and no local account of the lynching was found.

accounts.gist: Citizens of Wilkinson county lynched a Black burglar who had confessed to setting fire to a store in Woodville.

accounts.label: Lynching tallies
accounts.gist: An unknown Black man was lynched near Woodville, Miss., in May; the Black lists give the day as the 28th and the Wichita Searchlight gives the cause as arson.

accounts.label: Local paper on the fire
accounts.gist: The Woodville Republican described an incendiary fire that destroyed two stores and called for the 'guilty party, or parties' to be found, but its indexed issues found contain no report of the lynching.

framing.detail: A single neutral digest line, 'lynched a negro burglar who confessed', among unrelated national news.
Counted as 'Unknown, colored, near Woodville, Miss.' in a Providence Journal half-year tally of 45 lynchings.
The local paper called the fire the 'dirty, villainous work of the fire bug' and said it 'makes the blood boil', urging that the guilty be 'brought to justice'; it did not mention a lynching.
The Seattle Republican listed the case under 'Mobocracy's Bloody Reign' as part of 'Uncle Sam's' lynching record, comparing it to Russia and Turkey.
The Wichita Searchlight listed it by date, cause ('arson') and place without comment in the excerpt found.

Not reported; the confession implies he had been caught, but no report says whether officers held him
